INTRO_KICKER: For programming, public engagement, and marketing teams
INTRO_COL1: Oddtoe is an experiential design and generative-AI animation studio based in Melbourne, creating projection, installation, and animated work for events, venues, and galleries. This is a use case: how a museum uses Oddtoe for a museum late opening, from the first idea to the photographs people post that night. The worked example is one late, with one object in the atrium or the forecourt: projection, or an illuminated inflatable, live from dusk. The same steps apply to the sleepover, the school-holiday character, and the gala.
INTRO_COL2: Come to Oddtoe for a piece designed by an artist who has already put one in a City of Melbourne venue. For Babbling with Baobabs, a kids’ show at the Melbourne Comedy Festival in 2019, Oddtoe carved a 2.1-metre baobab and ran live projection over it at Signal, on Northbank. That is the shape of a late opening job: one object, one room full of people who did not come for the art, and a photograph they take anyway. The DJ and the bar can stay; the piece is what people stand in front of.
DRAWINGS_KICKER: Let's look at three steps in the process...
DRAWINGS_INTRO: Oddtoe handles the first three stages of a late opening piece: what the object is, how it is drawn into the building at scale, and how it hangs, plugs in, and gets past the people who look after the fabric of the building.
DRAW1_BODY: I do like this stage. What is the one thing in the atrium that a person who has never been to your museum photographs and posts? Projection on the far wall, a lit object hanging in the void, or something in the forecourt they walk past on the way in. The idea, and what it has to do with the exhibition that is on, get worked out here.
DRAW2_BODY: The piece gets drawn in the room, at scale, with the balustrades, the doorways and the view from the ticket desk. That drawing is what the exhibitions team and facilities sign off, so it shows where it stands, what it weighs and what is underneath it. Get the drawing right and the size of the thing hits you for the first time.
DRAW3_BODY: Working out what the piece plugs into and what it hangs from. Where the projector sits so nobody walks through the beam, how to find a rigging point in a building where you cannot drill a hole, and how it all comes down before the cleaners arrive. Oddtoe works this through with your facilities team before anything is built. Leave it until the afternoon of the late and you are solving it with the doors about to open.

CIRCLES_TITLE: 6 IDEAS FOR YOUR NEXT LATE, SLEEPOVER OR GALA
CIRCLES_SUB: Six jobs a programming team has in a year, each with one object at the centre. Roll over a circle and pick the one your museum could pull off.
CIRCLES_FOOT: Want one of these for your museum? Send the date and the room. Most of them start with a drawing of the building.
CIRCLE1_TITLE: The Thing In The Atrium After Dark
CIRCLE1_BODY: The late opening needs one object that people who came for the bar photograph anyway. Projection on the far wall, or an illuminated inflatable hanging in the void, live from dusk until close, and gone before the school groups arrive.
CIRCLE2_BODY: The sleepover is the same brief at child height. A walk-in object in the great hall, lit low, that a seven-year-old falls asleep looking at and talks about for a year. It packs away and comes out for the next one.
CIRCLE3_BODY: A drawn character for the school-holiday program: on the map, the activity sheet, the signage, and in costume on the day. Designed here, and a specialist maker builds the costume from the drawings.
CIRCLE4_BODY: Short animated pieces beside an object or a room, drawn in the museum’s own voice instead of stock footage. A minute long, on a loop, so the label does less of the work and the object does more.
CIRCLE5_BODY: Topiary, a sculpture or an inflatable that stands out the front for the run of the exhibition and comes down with it. Everyone who walks past knows something is on, whether or not they come in.
CIRCLE6_TITLE: The Thing The Donors Stand Next To
CIRCLE6_BODY: One object on the night of the gala, lit for the room, that every table photographs and the chair mentions in the speech. Afterwards it goes into the collection store, or back out for the next late.
WHO_KICKER: Programming, public engagement, marketing, and the friends
WHO_COL1: Museums, galleries, libraries, science centres and heritage houses with a public program. The person who rings is usually in programming, public engagement or marketing, and the job already has a date, a room and a budget line. Programming teams run a calendar: two or three big exhibitions, a late every month or season, school holidays, a sleepover and a gala. Each one needs something to happen in the building. Marketing needs a photograph that proves it happened, and people through the door who do not usually come.
WHO_COL2: Public engagement and learning teams want the kids’ character, the sleepover piece and the interpretation, and they want it to hold up in front of a class. The friends’ organisation and the development team want the gala centrepiece, and they want it still there for the members’ night. Oddtoe has put a piece in a City of Melbourne venue for a kids’ show, so approvals, rigging and the after-hours install are in the plan from the start. Agencies producing a late for a museum are welcome too: see experiential marketing.
TIMELINE_TITLE: A LATE OPENING, FROM BRIEF TO THE MORNING AFTER
TIMELINE_ARIA: Stages of a museum late opening
STEP1_TITLE: Every late has a bar and a DJ
STEP1_BODY: The bar is booked, the DJ is booked, the galleries stay open until ten, and it looks like every other museum late night in the city. The people you want are the ones who have never been in, and they come for whatever their friends posted last time. So before anything gets drawn we settle one question: what is the one thing in the building that night that someone photographs?
STEP1_CRAFT: A photograph first, then an object
STEP1_CAPTION: The brief, before anyone has drawn a thing
STEP2_TITLE: The piece, drawn in the room
STEP2_BODY: The object gets drawn into the atrium or the forecourt at the size it will be, with the balustrades, the doors and the view from the ticket desk. That drawing goes to the exhibitions team and to facilities, because they are the ones who have to say yes to the weight, the power and the rigging. You approve a picture of the thing in your building before anything is built.
STEP2_CAPTION: A carved form in the studio, before its finish goes on
STEP3_TITLE: Built to the drawings, wired for the building
STEP3_BODY: Design happens in Melbourne. A carved or built piece comes out of my own workshop; an inflatable comes from a specialist maker working from the drawings. Power, rigging points and heritage constraints get settled with your facilities team while the build is on, so nothing turns up that needs a hole drilled in a listed wall.
STEP3_CAPTION: Lights and projection tested before the install
STEP4_TITLE: In by the afternoon, live from dusk
STEP4_BODY: The piece goes in during the afternoon, after the last school group and before the doors open again. Projection is lined up in daylight and checked once it gets dark. Front-of-house staff get a short briefing on what it is and who to call, and then it runs until close.
STEP4_CRAFT: Lined up in daylight, run in the dark
STEP4_CAPTION: A carved piece lit deep red by projection
STEP5_TITLE: The posts, the press, and the report
STEP5_BODY: The photographs come from the crowd, and the museum shoots its own as well, so there is something to send to the press the next morning. Then the marketing team writes the report: the door against last year, first-time visitors, posts that tagged the museum, and memberships sold in the week after.
STEP5_CRAFT: Photos and video the museum owns
STEP5_CAPTION: Projection run live from a laptop on the night
STEP6_TITLE: Into the store, or on to the next venue
STEP6_BODY: A DJ is gone by Monday. A built piece goes into the collection store and comes out for the next late, the sleepover or the gala, or it tours to the next venue in its crate. One build across several nights is an easier line for a director to sign than a fresh hire each time.
STEP6_CRAFT: One build, used across the year
WHY_KICKER: The bit that is not a service
WHY_TITLE: Why Oddtoe Likes a Museum Late
WHY_COL1: I make my own work as well as client work, and installation art in a public building is the work I want to make more of. A museum late is about the only commission where the room, the lights going down and a crowd who did not come for the art are all handed to you on the same night. The baobab taught me that. It was built for a comedy show, and the tree had to work for children who had come for the jokes.
WHY_COL2: A museum also has the thing I care about most in a brief, which is a subject. There is an exhibition on, with objects and a story behind them, so the piece after dark can be about that instead of being about nothing. The practical upside for the museum is that the person designing the object has a stake in whether it works. I want the atrium to look right at ten o’clock for the same reason your marketing team does.

WYG_KICKER: Objects, drawings, and the footage afterwards
WYG_TITLE: What Does a Museum Actually Get?
WYG_COL1: The piece, the drawings it was approved from, the animation if it is projected, and the photos and video from the night. All of it is the museum’s to keep, crate included, and it comes out again for the next late. • The object — in this example one lit piece for the atrium or the forecourt • The drawings — plans and elevations facilities can file, and the next venue can work from • The animation — if the piece is projected, the sequences are yours to run again • Photos and video from the night, for the press and for the museum’s own channels
WYG_COL2: People tend to forget about the drawings. Facilities will ask for them the next time the piece goes up, and a partner venue will ask for them before it agrees to take it on tour. They are part of the job, so they arrive finished. It can be whatever the brief needs: a projection on the atrium wall, an illuminated inflatable in the void, a kinetic piece in the foyer, or a character for the school holidays, animated for the screens and built for the day. They are designed together, so what runs on the wall is the same thing that stands in the room.
PKG1_BODY: We work out what the night needs to look like before we work out what to build. Bring the date, the exhibition, and a plan of the room.
PKG2_KICKER: Drawn until you can see it
PKG2_BODY: The piece drawn in your atrium or forecourt at the size it will be, with people for scale. Exhibitions and facilities sign off on a picture of the thing in the building.
PKG3_BODY: Weight, rigging points, power, sightlines and what the heritage listing allows. Install after the last school group, and the date, which nobody can move.
PKG4_BODY: Designed in Melbourne, built by the right maker for the piece, here or near you. Finished to photograph under low light, and made to come down by morning and go back up for the next one.
PKG5_BODY: I run the job myself: visual progress reports, a plan against your date, and a run sheet for the afternoon worked out with your facilities and front-of-house teams.
CRED_KICKER: A precedent, in a City of Melbourne venue
CRED_TITLE: Why an Installation Artist Designs This
CRED_COL1: A late opening piece has to work three ways at once: as an installation in a room with a heritage listing, as a projection or a lit object that photographs after dark, and as something the museum can put up again. All three are the studio’s own ground. See installation art and projection art. Oddtoe has done it once already in a public venue. For Babbling with Baobabs at the Melbourne Comedy Festival in 2019, a kids’ show at Signal, the City of Melbourne’s arts space on Northbank, Oddtoe designed and built a 2.1-metre carved baobab and ran live projection over it through the show.
CRED_COL2: That job had what a late has: a venue with its own rules, projection lined up in daylight and run in the dark, and an audience who had come for something else. Children and their parents, there for the jokes, with a tree in the room that had to hold its own. For an inflatable in the void or a character for the school holidays, the design is done here and a specialist maker builds from the drawings. There is no delivered museum inflatable to show you yet, so what you get is the process, drawn out in full before you commit to it.

FAQ.q: What does this museum late opening use case cover?
FAQ.a: A worked example of a museum late opening. It follows one brief - a late with a bar, a DJ and nothing to photograph - from the first question through design, fabrication, the night itself, and what the museum still owns afterwards. The example is one lit object in the atrium or the forecourt. The sleepover piece, the school-holiday character, the exhibition animation, the forecourt piece and the gala centrepiece follow the same shape.

FAQ.q: How long does a museum late opening piece take?
FAQ.a: Six to eight weeks from brief to the night for a carved or built piece. The drawings for facilities come first, then fabrication, then the install on the afternoon of the late. An illuminated inflatable takes longer, because a specialist maker builds it from the drawings. If your late is closer than that, say so, and we work out what fits.

FAQ.q: What does a museum late opening piece cost?
FAQ.a: Oddtoe does not publish prices. Cost is driven by what the piece is, how large, whether it is projected or built, how it hangs, and whether it travels. It is costed the same way as any other prop fabrication job. Send the date, the room and the exhibition and you get a quote.

FAQ.q: Can it tour to another venue?
FAQ.a: Yes. Pieces are designed to crate, and the drawings go with them, so a partner venue can see what it weighs and where it hangs before it agrees. If it leaves the country, freight and customs get worked through with a freight agent as part of the job. Often the simpler answer for a venue overseas is to build near them, working from the drawings.

FAQ.q: Can we use it again, or does it stay?
FAQ.a: Either. It can go into the collection store and come out for the next late, the sleepover or the gala, or it can stand for the run of an exhibition and come down with it. Used a few times, one build can cost less than hiring something new for each night.

FAQ.q: Can you do the animation and projection as well?
FAQ.a: Yes, and they are designed together when the brief calls for it - the object and the animation projected over it, or short animated interpretation beside an exhibit. See projection art and generative AI animation.
Oddtoe is based in Melbourne, Australia. Supplier and business contacts run through Berlin and Los Angeles, and those are the starting points for work in Europe and the United States.
